title: Mitochondria
subtitle: Class 9 · The Fundamental Unit of Life

elements.text: What pays for every move you make?

elements.alt: An animal cell with its membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and several mitochondria scattered through it
A mitochondrion cut open: an outer membrane, an inner membrane folded into cristae, and the matrix inside, holding ribosomes and a loop of mitochondrial DNA
A close-up of one crista: the folded inner membrane studded with ATP synthase on both faces, the matrix outside the fold and the intermembrane space inside it

elements.text: Somewhere in here. These orange capsules are mitochondria — a cell has hundreds.
One of them, cut open. Two membranes, and everything else sits between them.
The outer membrane: smooth, and the boundary with the rest of the cell.
Just inside it, a second membrane — and this one does not stay smooth.
It folds inward. One fold is a crista. Many are cristae.
The space the folds sit in is the matrix — a thick fluid packed with enzymes.
Zoom into one fold. Those studs are ATP synthase — the machines that build ATP.
Look in the matrix: its own ribosomes, and its own loop of DNA.

Fold a bedsheet into a small box. The sheet is still the same size — the folds do not shrink it, they fit more of it into the same space.

Cristae do exactly that with membrane. And ATP is built ON that membrane, so more folds means more surface, and more surface means more ATP.
No other organelle except the chloroplast carries its own DNA. Which is why biologists think a mitochondrion was once a free-living bacterium that moved into a bigger cell and never left.

elements.caption: How many mitochondria one cell holds

elements.text: More folds = more surface = more ATP

Your turn, and answer before I do.

A heart muscle cell holds about twenty-five times as many mitochondria as a skin cell. Say why, in one sentence.
Two membranes. The inner one folds.

beats.topic: Why a cell needs a power plant
beats.narration: Every time you lift your hand, something inside your cells paid for it. Muscles do not run on food directly — they run on one molecule, and there is a specific place in the cell where that molecule gets built. Let's go and find it.

beats.topic: Where mitochondria sit in a cell
beats.narration: This is an animal cell. The big circle on the left is the nucleus. And these orange capsules scattered through it are what we came for — mitochondria. A single cell does not have one. It has hundreds.

So let's take one and cut it open. Straight away you can see the thing that makes a mitochondrion unusual: it has two membranes, one inside the other. Almost nothing else in the cell is built that way.
Start at the edge. The outer membrane is smooth, and it is the boundary between the mitochondrion and the rest of the cell. Nothing complicated yet — it is a bag.
Now look just inside it. There is a second membrane, and the thin gap between the two has a name of its own — the intermembrane space. But watch what this inner one does that the outer one does not.

beats.topic: Cristae are folds of the inner membrane
beats.narration: It folds inward. Each of these fingers pushing into the middle is a fold of that same inner membrane — not a separate part sitting inside it, a fold of it. One fold is called a crista. Many of them are cristae.

Here is why that matters, and if you remember one thing from today, make it this. Fold a bedsheet into a small box. The sheet is still the same size — the folds do not shrink it, they fit more of it into the same space. Cristae do exactly that with membrane. And ATP is built on that membrane, so more folds means more surface, and more surface means more ATP.
The space those folds sit in is the matrix. It is not empty — it is a thick fluid packed with enzymes, and a lot of the chemistry of respiration happens right here.

beats.topic: ATP synthase on the folded membrane
beats.narration: Let's zoom right into one fold. Those studs along both faces are ATP synthase — tiny machines standing on the membrane, and each one builds ATP. Now you can see why surface area is the whole story: every extra bit of fold is room for more of these.

So the whole path looks like this. Glucose from your food is broken down in the cytoplasm into pyruvate. The pyruvate comes into the mitochondrion, oxygen is used at the cristae, and out comes ATP — the molecule your muscles actually spend.
Write this down, because everything else follows from it. More folds, more surface, more ATP.

beats.topic: Cells that work harder hold more
beats.narration: And here is the proof that it matters. A heart muscle cell, which never stops working, holds around five thousand mitochondria. A skin cell holds about two hundred. Same body, same DNA — the difference is how much ATP the cell has to spend.
One more thing, and it is genuinely strange. Look back in the matrix. Those small dots are ribosomes, and that little loop is DNA — the mitochondrion's own.

No other organelle except the chloroplast carries its own DNA. Which is why biologists think a mitochondrion was once a free-living bacterium that moved into a bigger cell and never left. You are, in a small way, carrying a guest.
Your turn now, and answer before I do. A heart muscle cell holds about twenty-five times as many mitochondria as a skin cell. Say why, in one sentence.

So: two membranes. The inner one folds into cristae. Folding buys surface area, surface area buys ATP, and the cells that spend the most ATP carry the most mitochondria. Remember the folding and the rest follows.
